dok_rationale: Part (c) compares two designs against a causal claim, links random assignment, control, and blinding to specific threats, explains a concrete alternative cause, and bounds generalization from volunteers.
stem: Suppose a researcher recruits 30 student volunteers to study whether an energy drink changes reaction time.\par\smallskip \textbf{Design 1:} The first 15 students to sign up receive the energy drink; the last 15 receive water. A tester who knows each drink measures reaction time.\par \textbf{Design 2:} A coin flip assigns each volunteer to the energy drink or water. The water is flavored to match, both drinks are served in identical opaque cups, and neither the volunteer nor the tester knows which drink was assigned.
first_take: Which design would make you more willing to attribute a reaction-time difference to the drink? Name one feature behind your choice.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the experimental units, explanatory variable and its levels, and response variable.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For each design, state whether it has random assignment, a control group, and blinding. Explain one job performed by each feature.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which design could support the claim that the energy drink caused a reaction-time difference? Cite the specific features that settle it, explain what a difference under Design 1 could be due to instead, and decide whether either result could automatically generalize to all teenagers.

answers.a: Experimental units: the 30 student volunteers. Explanatory variable: assigned drink, with levels energy drink and matched water. Response variable: measured reaction time, with its recorded time unit.
answers.b: Design 1 has a water control and replication but no random assignment or blinding. Design 2 has coin-flip random assignment, a matched water control, replication, and double blinding. Random assignment tends to balance lurking variables; the control supplies a comparison; blinding reduces expectancy and measurement effects.
answers.c: Design 2 can support causation for these volunteers because the coin flip randomly assigns treatments, both groups are compared, and blinding limits placebo or tester effects. Under Design 1, early volunteers could differ from late volunteers in motivation, sleep, schedule, or baseline reaction time, so signup order could explain the difference. Neither design automatically generalizes to all teenagers because the 30 participants volunteered and were not randomly selected or shown to represent all teenagers.

expectedElements.description: Chooses Design 2 and identifies coin-flip random assignment as the central causal feature
Explains how the matched control and blinding strengthen the comparison beyond assignment alone
Names a plausible early-versus-late volunteer difference and links it to reaction time
States that volunteers do not automatically represent all teenagers despite random treatment assignment

scoringGuide.E: Chooses Design 2 with random assignment, control, and blinding explained, gives a linked signup-order alternative for Design 1, and limits generalization from volunteers.
scoringGuide.P: Chooses Design 2 and names key features but incompletely explains the alternative cause or population limit, or treats blinding as the causal feature while barely addressing assignment.
scoringGuide.I: Chooses Design 1 because it has equal group sizes, claims a control alone establishes cause, or generalizes to all teenagers because 30 people participated.

commonMistakes: Calling Design 1 randomized because students arrived in an unpredictable order
Treating equal group sizes as a substitute for random assignment
Saying identical cups alone blind participants without the matched drink and concealed assignment
Confusing random assignment among volunteers with random selection of teenagers
